title: The Man Who Pointed
author: Lantern Original
summaryTr: Zaman turlarının en önemli kuralı basit: Hiç kimse fotoğrafa girmeyecek. Ama genç rehber Ayla'nın ilk turunda, tarihin en ünlü fotoğraflarından biri tam gözlerinin önünde çekilmek üzeredir.
paragraphs: Ayla Demir had only one rule for her first tour, and she repeated it four times before the group even reached the Door. Nobody gets in the photograph.
Three hours later, she would be begging a tourist to break it.

It was the golden rule of Yesterday Tours. In the year 2147, anybody with enough money could spend one afternoon in the past. They could look, listen and breathe the old air. They could not touch things, talk to local people, or stand in front of a camera. A photograph from 1923 can still hang in a museum a hundred and twenty years later. If a stranger with the wrong clothes and the wrong face is standing in it, historians start asking questions. And questions, the company said, were how history changed.

Today's destination was Port Alder, 14 June 1923: Airship Day. It was the biggest day in the town's history. Port Alder was also the home town of Ayla's mother's family, the Marshes, so Ayla had asked for this tour herself.

There were four tourists. Mr. and Mrs. Nakamura were seventy years old and very polite, and they held hands all the time. Kofi was sixteen, with a quiet smile; his grandfather had paid for him to come. The fourth was Mr. Peterson, who had paid double for "the best seat in history" and expected the whole past to arrange itself around him.

Before they left, Ayla gave everyone a grey wool coat and a hat from 1923. Mr. Peterson held his coat between two fingers, as if it was a dead animal. "It itches," he said. Under it he was wearing his own jacket, which was bright orange and had a shiny silver zip down the front.
"Please keep the coat on, Mr. Peterson."
"Of course," said Mr. Peterson, and he did not.
The Door looked like a plain metal frame in a white room. When Ayla pressed the green button, the air inside it became soft and silver, like water. One by one, the tourists stepped through.

They came out in a narrow alley behind the fish market in Port Alder. It was five to three on a warm afternoon. The air smelled of fish, coal smoke and horses. Somewhere near, a band was playing badly and very happily. Mr. Peterson threw his coat onto a box and walked out of the alley in his orange jacket, and Ayla had to run after him.

The whole town had come to the harbour. Men wore their best hats, women carried umbrellas against the sun, and children sat on their fathers' shoulders. In forty-five minutes, the airship Silver Whale would arrive, the first passenger airship ever to visit Port Alder. At twenty to four, the mayor would make a speech, the band would play louder, and the town's famous photographer, Edith Holloway, would take pictures from the right end of the harbour wall.

That was why Ayla's route stayed on the left side, as far from the camera as possible. She had checked it a hundred times on her tablet, where the photographer was only a small red circle. "Stay together," she told the group. "Stay on the left. Look, listen, enjoy."
At twenty-five past three, she counted her tourists. One, two, three. She counted again. Three.
"Of course," she said.
She found him on the right side of the harbour, the wrong side, holding a hot pie. He was standing next to a red-and-white ticket booth. And when Ayla saw the booth, her stomach turned cold.

She knew that booth. She knew the crooked lamp-post next to it. She knew the camera on its wooden legs, twenty metres away, and the small woman with her head under a black cloth. And in front of the booth stood a little girl in a blue dress, with a white ribbon in her hair and a red apple in her hand.

Ayla had seen this place a hundred times. It hung in the Port Alder museum. It was in every school book in her mother's town. It was the most famous photograph in the history of the town, and its name was The Man Who Pointed.

In the photograph, a man in a pale, shiny jacket stands with one arm up and his mouth open, pointing at the sky. Next to his knee, a small girl with a white ribbon looks up too. Nobody in a hundred and twenty years had found out who the man was. Under the picture, the museum card always said the same thing: Moments after this photograph was taken, a heavy iron hook fell from the airship's rope. It hit the ground exactly where the girl had been standing. Nobody was hurt.
In a black-and-white picture, an orange jacket looks pale. And a silver zip looks like a line of light.
"Oh, no," whispered Ayla. "Oh, no, no, no."
The Man Who Pointed was Mr. Peterson. The worst tourist in the world was the most famous stranger in Port Alder's history.
She looked at her watch. It was 3.38.
"Mr. Peterson," she said, trying to sound calm. "We need to stay here for a few minutes."
"I'm bored," said Mr. Peterson. "I'm hot. This pie is mostly pastry. Everyone is wearing silly hats, and I have seen enough. I'm going back to the alley."

He started to walk away. Ayla's mind was working very fast. If he left now, there would be no man in the photograph. There would be no shout. Nobody would be looking at the sky. The hook would fall on a six-year-old girl, and a hundred and twenty years later, the picture on the museum wall would change, or disappear, or something much worse. She could not take the risk.
"Mr. Peterson, wait." She took a breath. "In two minutes, something is going to happen that nobody from our time has ever seen. You paid for the best seat in history. This is the seat."
He looked at her. He looked at his pie. "Two minutes," he said.
"Two minutes."

At twenty to four exactly, the Silver Whale came round the end of the harbour wall, and the whole town screamed with joy. It was enormous, as long as a street, silver and shining against the blue sky. Four ropes fell from its nose, and men ran forward to catch them. At the end of each rope hung an iron hook as big as a bucket.
Ayla stood behind Mr. Peterson and held his sleeve. The Nakamuras and Kofi had followed her, and now they were watching the airship with their mouths open. She looked at her watch. 3.41.

Above them, something went wrong with the machine that held the ropes. She heard a sharp metal sound, and one rope began to slide. The hook at the end of it started to fall, slowly at first, and then very fast.

Nobody saw it. Everyone was looking at the front of the airship, laughing and waving. Mr. Peterson was looking at his pie. And the little girl in the blue dress, with her apple in her hand and her mouth open in wonder, was standing exactly under the hook.

Ayla could run. She could reach the girl in three seconds. Her whole body wanted to do it. But the photograph said: the man points. The girl stands next to him. The girl moves a moment later. If Ayla ran, the photograph would no longer be true, and she did not know what happened to a world where a true thing became false.
She took Mr. Peterson's right arm and pushed it up into the air. "Mr. Peterson!" she shouted in his ear. "Look up! Now!"
He looked up. For one second, his face had no expression at all. Then he saw the hook, and he opened his mouth.
"LOOK OUT!" he screamed. "THE HOOK! GET BACK! GET BACK!"

His arm was pointing straight at the sky. People turned. A woman screamed and pulled the little girl backwards into her arms. The crowd opened like a door. And then the hook hit the ground with a crash that shook the harbour, and broke the stones, and sent up a cloud of dust, exactly where the girl had been standing.
Behind them, a camera clicked.
For a long moment, nobody moved. Then a man's voice shouted, "Who is that? The man in the orange jacket!" Hundreds of faces turned. A policeman in a tall hat began to push through the crowd.
"Run," said Ayla.

It was 3.43. The Door would open in the alley at 3.50, and it would stay open for exactly one minute. Mr. Peterson, who had not run since school, ran like a champion. They went through the fish market, over a table of crabs, under a horse, and round a very angry woman with a basket. Mrs. Nakamura lost her hat, and Kofi picked it up without stopping. Behind them, a whistle blew again and again.

At 3.49, they fell into the alley. At 3.50, the air between the walls turned silver and soft. The policeman appeared at the end of the alley, red in the face. "Stop!" he shouted. "In the name of the King!"
Ayla counted her people. One, two, three, four. Then she jumped, and the last thing she saw of 1923 was a tall hat and a very surprised face.
Back in the white room, the tourists lay on the floor. Mrs. Nakamura laughed until she cried. Kofi lifted both fists in the air. "Best. Tour. Ever," he said.
Mr. Peterson did not say anything for a long time. At last he looked up. "The little girl," he said. "Is she all right?"
"She's fine."
"You can't know that."
"Yes," said Ayla. "I can."
Two days later he sent her a message: Take me to see the photograph. So they went to the museum in Port Alder, just the two of them, and stood in front of the glass.

It was all there. The red-and-white booth. The crooked lamp-post. A man in a bright jacket, with his arm in the air and his mouth open. He looked frightened and brave at the same time. And behind his shoulder, almost hidden, was a young woman in a dark hat. She had one hand on his arm, and she was pushing it upwards. Her face was only a pale shadow. Ayla had seen that shadow a hundred times and had never once wondered about it.
"That's you," said Mr. Peterson.
"Yes."
"But you said nobody gets in the photograph."
"That's the rule," said Ayla. "It's just not always true."
She read the museum card again. This time, she read the last line slowly. The girl with the white ribbon was called Lily Marsh. She lived to be ninety-one, and she had four children.

In Ayla's family, people had a saying. When something went well, they said: "Thank the stranger." Nobody knew why. Ayla's mother said it every birthday. Ayla's grandmother had said it every New Year. Ayla had always thought it was just a funny way of speaking.
"Nobody will ever believe me," said Mr. Peterson quietly. "I'm the Man Who Pointed, and nobody will believe me."
"No," said Ayla. "They won't."
She looked at the small girl, at the white ribbon, at the red apple in her hand. Then she whispered, very softly, so that only the photograph could hear:
"You're welcome."

glossary.door: Kapı (hikâyede: zamanda yolculuk için kullanılan geçit)

quiz.q: What is the most important rule of Yesterday Tours?
quiz.explainTr: Şirketin altın kuralı: Hiç kimse fotoğrafa girmeyecek. Çünkü fotoğraflar yüzyıllarca saklanır ve tarihi değiştirebilir.

quiz.q: Why is Ayla afraid when she sees the red-and-white booth?
options: She recognizes the place from a famous photograph
quiz.explainTr: Ayla kırmızı-beyaz bilet kabini ve eğri lamba direğini 'İşaret Eden Adam' fotoğrafından tanır.

quiz.q: Why does Ayla not run to save the little girl herself?
options: She does not see the hook
She wants Mr. Peterson to be a hero
She wants the photograph to stay true
quiz.explainTr: Ayla, fotoğrafı değiştirmekten korkar; fotoğrafta adam işaret ediyor ve küçük kız bir an sonra kenara çekiliyor.

quiz.q: What does Ayla do when the hook starts to fall?
options: She pushes Mr. Peterson's arm up and tells him to look up
She takes a photograph of the airship
quiz.explainTr: Ayla Bay Peterson'ın kolunu yukarı kaldırır ve yukarı bakmasını söyler; Peterson da bağırarak herkesi uyarır.

quiz.q: Who is the little girl with the white ribbon?
quiz.explainTr: Kızın adı Lily Marsh'tır ve Ayla'nın annesinin ailesinden, yani Ayla'nın atalarındandır.
